unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
$(u\cdot\nabla)v$ is vector calculus notation for the vector field with entries
\[
[(u\cdot\nabla)v]_j=\sum_{i=1}^2u_i\frac{\partial v_j}{\partial x_i},\quad j=1,2.
\]
(2)
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Componentwise convection used by B and the physical PDE; ambient vector calculus is retained rather than reconstructed from a library.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: We assume the viscosity $\nu>0$ and forcing $f\in V$ to be known, possibly determined beforehand by independent experiments (theory for these distinct inverse problems could be developed as well, for $\nu$ for instance following ideas in [17, 31]). In contrast, and following common practice in data assimilation, we assume that the initial condition $\theta=u(0)$ of the system is unknown.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Statistical parameter scope: viscosity and forcing are known. Theorems 2 and 4 specialize to nu=1/2,f=0; the initial condition is the inferential target.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Let us emphasise that the ‘white’ noise $\varepsilon_i$ in (19) is purely of measurement error type (arising from the discretisation of $u_\theta$) and that we do not model explicit stochasticity in the Navier-Stokes dynamics itself, in particular we do not consider a SPDE model.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: The observation model has random measurement noise and design, while its forward PDE is deterministic.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: By convention we regard the first $N$ measurements as the training sample and the additional pair $(X_{N+1},t)$ as the prediction sample, where $X_{N+1}$ is drawn at random from $\lambda_\Omega$ and $t\in(0,T_p],T_p\geq T$, is a (deterministic) time we wish to fore- or hind-cast.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Prediction horizon convention. Theorem 3 separately prints capital P in T_P in prose and lowercase p in display bounds.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
If we denote by $\theta_0$ the ground truth initial condition that generated the data (19) and by $\theta\sim\Pi(\cdot\mid Z^{(N)})$ a draw from the posterior distribution, then this leads us to consider the posterior quadratic ‘prediction risk’
\[
E_{X_{N+1}}\left(|u_\theta(t,X_{N+1})-u_{\theta_0}(t,X_{N+1})|^2\right)=\|u_\theta(t,\cdot)-u_{\theta_0}(t,\cdot)\|_{L^2(\Omega)^2}^2,\quad t>0,
\]
(22)
which measures how well we predict on average the state of the system at time $t$ and at a ‘generic’ position $X_{N+1}\sim\lambda_\Omega$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Interpretation of trajectory error. The uniform spatial law and the page-4 Lebesgue L2 convention raise a volume-normalization issue. This explanatory identity is not substituted for the unsquared theorem error norms.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Moreover, for $u(0)\ne v(0)\in V$, the ratio in (15) is always finite, so a constant $c_P$ always exists in this case. For the statistical results below we require however uniform control of $c_P$ in the parameter space of admissible initial conditions $u(0),v(0)$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Remark 1 distinguishes a pair-dependent inverse-Poincare constant from a uniform restriction. Theorem 1B has the former explicit ratio; Theorem 5 uses a projected prior, not an independently asserted global bound.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
For instance suppose both $u(0),v(0)\in V$ have a finite expansion in the $H$-orthonormal eigen-basis $(e_j:j\geq0)$ of the Stokes operator $A$ (see (20) below), up to ‘frequency’ $J$. Then
\[
\frac{\|u(0)-v(0)\|_V^2}{\|u(0)-v(0)\|_{L^2}^2}=\frac{\sum_{j\leq J}\lambda_j\langle e_j,u(0)-v(0)\rangle_{L^2}^2}{\sum_{j\leq J}\langle e_j,u(0)-v(0)\rangle_{L^2}^2}\leq\lambda_J\equiv c_P.
\]
Observe that one has the asymptotic distribution $\lambda_j\simeq j$ as $j\to\infty$, of the eigenvalues of the Stokes operator $A$ in $d=2$, see Proposition 4.14 in [8].
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: The source bounds a squared norm ratio by lambda_J and calls it c_P, whereas (15) defines an unsquared ratio. Preserve both displays and do not change the theorem exponential.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Examples of ‘base priors’ $\Pi'$ with $\mathcal H=(V\cap H^\alpha(\Omega)^2,\|\cdot\|_{H^\alpha(\Omega)^2})$ for any $\alpha\geq2$ can be easily constructed:
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Illustration after Condition 1, not an equality required of every admissible prior RKHS. General Condition 1 only imposes continuous embedding.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
Then the conclusions of Theorem 3 remain true with convergence rate
\[
\eta_N=(\log N)^\beta\times N^{-\alpha/(2\alpha+2)},\quad\text{some }\beta>0.
\]
unranked_auxiliary_passages.scope_note: Theorem 5 explicitly inherits Theorem 3 conclusions: both posterior concentration events and the posterior-mean/trajectory error. This is a statement reference, unlike the proof-only use of Theorem 1 or 2 by other results. Prior projection and rate replace their counterparts; no unprinted lower growth bound on J_N is inserted.

source_issues.description: The source is the registered 19-page arXiv v3 stamped 9 Jul 2024. It is not assumed identical to the published AoS text.
The source permits X instead of X^2 for vector fields. L2(Omega)^2 in Theorem 3 is a vector-space subscript, whereas the squared norms in (22) and Remark 1 have an external square.
The PDE space H of divergence-free zero-mean fields differs from the Gaussian RKHS calligraphic H. V uses the gradient norm, not the full inhomogeneous H1 norm.
The main-text Sobolev definition covers integer m, while Condition 1 permits real alpha>=2. Fractional periodic Sobolev and RKHS constructions are standard external notions not expanded here.

The main text defines strong by equality of (10) in H rather than just V-prime, but refers to external books for complete solution-theory details. Theorem 1 expressly specifies C([0,T],V); no other theorem gains an extra regularity premise by importing a proof.

The Lp display does not separately state strong measurability, and the L-infinity prose says time-bounded without specifying essential versus pointwise boundedness. Ordinary Bochner and function-space conventions remain external.

Theorem 1 includes coincident initial conditions but writes logarithms and ratios involving solution discrepancies. It does not explicitly define the zero-denominator limiting conventions for (14) or (15).

Equation (15) bounds an unsquared norm ratio and (16) contains exp(c2*cP). Remark 1 instead bounds the squared ratio by lambda_J and labels that bound c_P. The displays are preserved rather than reconciled by changing exponents.
Theorem 2 writes c-prime=c-prime(c,t) without introducing c in the statement. Comparability constants and their time/index uniformity are not further expanded there.
The lower bound in (18) uses log(1/discrepancy) for all positive times and natural-number indices without separately stating positivity or nonzero-denominator conventions.
The likelihood (21) writes u_theta(X_i,t_i), whereas (19) and the forward model use u_theta(t_i,X_i). The reversal is retained in the original passage.
Condition 1 uses theta=theta-prime/N^(1/(2alpha+2)); this is not the posterior contraction rate and the RKHS is that of the base prior. Sample-size dependence is retained.
The source declares the normally empty interval (T0,T] to mean {T} when T0=T>0 and uses a Dirac temporal law. This explicit exception must not be dropped.
Theorem 3 allows T0=0, while Theorem 4 requires T0>0. Theorem 5 inherits the observation setting of the conclusions it references; no minimax lower bound is asserted at T0=0.
Theorem 3 writes T_P in its prose but T_p in both displayed suprema. The preceding prediction convention also uses T_p. Preserve source case without silently rewriting the theorem.

Equation (22) identifies expectation under the uniform probability law on [0,2pi]^2 with a Lebesgue L2 norm squared without showing a volume factor. Page 4 explicitly names Lebesgue measure dx; the original equality is preserved.
Theorem 3 evaluates the PDE at the posterior mean initial condition. Nonlinearity does not permit replacing this with the posterior mean of the solution field.
Theorem 4 uses a ball radius U and positive c(U,T) without locally quantifying U>0. The preceding Proposition 1 has its own U>0; it is not silently imported as a new theorem hypothesis.
Theorem 5 says span E_J but writes E_J={e_j:j<=J}. The intended linear-span wording and the literal set notation are both retained, rather than silently replacing the original display.
Theorem 5 only states J_N=O(log log N); this upper bound alone does not ensure growth to infinity or eventual inclusion of a fixed J0. No lower growth condition is added to the source.

Equation (20) gives complex Fourier fields only up to proportionality; adjacent prose refers to real parts. Normalization, sine/cosine selection, lattice redundancy and eigenvalue-multiplicity ordering are not fully specified there.

Theorem 5 expressly reuses the conclusions of Theorem 3 with a projected prior and different rate. This must resolve all three conclusions, including the mean and forecast, without importing proof-only theorem references as extra dependencies.
